slides.sub: And you were not in the room.

slides.body:
Hit the numbers. Took the extra project. Stayed late. Said yes.

And the role went to someone who talks about the work less than you do.

Someone describes you in one sentence.
Everyone nods.
The decision is made.
You hear about it on Tuesday.

In that room, someone sums you up in a line. The line gets repeated. The line gets promoted.

You have never heard it.
Decide what you want said about you. Then make it true in the three conversations you keep postponing: the ask, the boundary, the honest feedback.
As an HR executive I know what gets said when your name comes up, what gets repeated, and what gets someone the role. I walk alongside you with what I have seen.

**1.** Write the one sentence you want a decision maker to say about you.
**2.** Ask one trusted peer what sentence they would actually say.
**3.** Name the difference.

That difference is your inside work.

Another year of good work, hoping somebody notices.

Hope has never had a seat in that room.

slides.sub: Here is the four-word question that fixes it.

slides.body:
Said in a review. Nodded at. Never explained.

And you spend a year trying to fix something nobody defined.
It feels like a judgment about who you are. It is usually a sentence someone could not finish.

Four words. Said calmly.

The most useful question in your career, and most people never ask it.

And that tells you something. If they cannot name one moment, the feedback is a feeling, and feelings can be reshaped.

If they can, you finally have something real to work on.

When feedback comes out of left field, I say: help me understand what strategic would have looked like in that meeting. I might have a blind spot. I am big enough to own it.

But I need the example to fix it.

slides.kicker: Try this at your next one-on-one
slides.body:
**1.** Thank them for the feedback.
**2.** Ask: can you give me an example?
**3.** Write the answer down, with the date.

That is your development plan. It is also your record.

Another year of guessing what they meant.

Guessing is not inside work.

posts.source: Dawn, Jun 18 2026 call (inspect what you expect)
posts.caption:
Here is a leadership habit I learned early and have never regretted.

Before you correct someone, go look. Not at what a peer told you. Not at what you assume. At the work itself. You inspect what you expect, and then you have the conversation from facts.

It takes ten more minutes. It saves you a good employee, and it saves you from being the leader who manages by rumor.

Leaders: what is one thing you expect from your team that you have not personally inspected this month?

slides.sub: I know. Follow me for a second.

slides.body:
If the first five hundred produce five solid candidates, nobody reads the rest.

Not because the rest were weaker. Because the pile was already full.
And the table is decided by who knows your name before your resume arrives.
You would never do that with your money.
One conversation a week with someone who does not sign your paycheck. Peers at other companies. Former colleagues. The person who interviewed you and said no.

Not the better resume. The one somebody in the building could vouch for.

That is how it actually goes. It is not unfair. It is how trust works.

**1.** Three people outside your company you have not spoken to in six months.
**2.** Two people inside you want to know better.
**3.** Send one message today. Not an ask. A hello.
That is the one week it does not work.
